title: Trump welcomes Mecca defence pact between Saudi, Pakistan, Turkey; says ‘shows how the Middle East is coming together’
content:
US President Donald Trump on Sunday (local time) welcomed the recently signed defence pact between Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan, saying that it shows how the Middle East is coming together. He made these remarks in a Truth Social post and wrote, "Very happy to see that Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan have recently, and finally, signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement. It shows how the Middle East is coming together, and how Countries will finally be able to defend themselves in a more meaningful way. Congratulations to the Great Leadership of the three Nations mentioned. THIS IS A BIG, BOLD, AND IMPORTANT FIRST STEP — WOW! " way agreement was signed on 7 August and comes against the backdrop of the ongoing US-Iran war, which has intensified violence across the region, including attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels. According to a Reuters report, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in Mecca, pledging closer military cooperation as security concerns grow in the Middle East. An official statement said the three-way agreement aims to strengthen collective deterrence and provides that an armed attack on any one of the three countries would be considered an attack on all. The statement said, "The Agreement is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression, and stipulates that any armed attack against any one of the three States shall be regarded as an attack against them all. It further provides for the enhancement of all aspects of defence cooperation among the three States." The agreement does not outline any specific military commitments or obligations. However, it states that its broader aim is to strengthen peace, stability and security in the region and beyond. This is a developing story. More details awaited. title: Iran's 134% food inflation bites hard: Meat, coffee and dairy quietly disappear from household tables
content:
People in Iran have reportedly cut back on meat, dairy and coffee, among other food items, as pressure on household finances continues amid Tehran's prolonged war with the United States. Iran is struggling with a crippling economy, with hyperinflation mounting economic strain at home. Multiple reports have suggested that the war ruined tens of millions of households in Iran. "Prices are up somewhere between 60 and 88% over the year, food has passed triple-digit inflation for the poorest households, and jobs - particularly full-time jobs and industrial work - are fewer," one of the reports claimed. As the West Asia war seems to have no end in sight, here's what Iran's economy looks like as of now. Iran’s year-on-year inflation rate remains above 80%, keeping pressure on household finances despite a decline in monthly inflation following recent currency and war shocks, ISNA reported on Saturday, 15 August. At the end of July 2026, the Statistical Center of Iran (SCI) had recorded its fifth consecutive month of record annual inflation. In a report released on 29 July, the Statistical Center put the 12-month inflation rate for the year ending in July at 66% for Iranian households, up from 62% in June. The SCI described it as the highest annual rate in decades. Meanwhile, data cited by Trade Economics, sourced from the SCI, showed that Iran's point-to-point/year-on-year inflation rate eased to 87.9% in July 2026 from 88.6% in June, marking the first slowdown in three months. However, the Central Bank of Iran recorded the twelve-month inflation at 61.4%, well below the SCI figure, according to NIAC insights. While the exact number is contested, the upward direction of inflation is the same in both reports. The 87.9% point-to-point rate — the change in prices in July against the same month a year earlier — meant the average household paid roughly 88% more for the same basket of goods and services it bought a year ago. Meanwhile, food prices remain the principal driver of overall inflation, even as annual food inflation was recorded in triple digits for a sixth consecutive month. In July, food inflation reached 134% nationwide and 140% in rural areas. More than two-thirds of the food items monitored by the statistical agency now exceed what economists describe as crisis-level inflation, Iran International reported on 5 August. Not just food, but prices rose sharply across other sectors, the report added. It claimed that household appliances were estimated to cost 114% more than a year ago, while transportation costs climbed 103%. Economists had then warned that a possible gasoline price increase could push food inflation even higher by raising distribution and delivery costs. They told Iran International that the figures reflect not only declining purchasing power and weaker job security but also rising uncertainty that makes long-term financial planning increasingly difficult for households. According to the Paytm currency converter, $1 was equal to IRR 1,374,587.50382 on 16 August. However, AlanChand.com showed the price of the US Dollar in the market was 1,862,500 Iranian Rials. "The price of US Dollar in Iranian Rials continued its downward trend...Compared to a week ago, the price has seen a 0.32 percent increase. Over the past six months, the price has experienced a 15.61 percent increase," the report added. Annual dairy consumption fell from around 130 kilograms per person in 2010 to just 40 kilograms today, Iran International reported, quoting Ali Ehsan Zafari, head of Iran's Dairy Cooperatives Union, as saying on 9 August. The report came as the latest figures from the SCI reportedly showed that dairy products cost around 147% more in July than a year earlier. Declining purchasing power also pushed households away from more expensive sources of animal protein. The report added that prices of beef, lamb and chicken were all around 149% higher in July than a year earlier, according to the SCI. The latest increases follow the recent war, which added to existing inflationary pressures and accelerated price rises across basic goods. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) data showed that Iran's red meat supply fell to approximately 623,000 metric tons last year, around 20% lower than in 2024 and nearly 39% below its 2010 level. For years, households unable to afford beef and lamb could turn to chicken. Per capita poultry consumption has risen by roughly 40% since 2010, suggesting that households have increasingly substituted chicken for more expensive beef and lamb. The sharp increase in poultry prices now threatens that fallback, while the collapse in dairy consumption suggests even relatively basic sources of animal protein are becoming harder for many families to afford. Besides, prices for oils and fats rose about 278% in June. Moreover, coffee consumption in Iran has also increasingly become an unaffordable luxury. Although global coffee prices declined, the cost of coffee beans in Iran — largely imported through the United Arab Emirates before the war — has nearly doubled compared to pre-war levels. The increase directly affected café prices. With rents and other expenses also rising, the price of a cup of coffee in some cafés has climbed by as much as four times. An Americano at cafés reviewed by Iran International started at about 1.1 million rials ($0.59) and reached roughly 3.8 million rials ($2.04) at some establishments. Espresso prices exceeded 3 million rials ($1.61) in some cases. Breakfast dishes started at around 2 million rials ($1.08) at some cafés, while options such as omelettes or bread with cheese and herbs could cost more than 4 million rials ($2.15). One said two drinks and a slice of cake for two people now cost about 12 million rials ($6.45). Another calculated that buying only a morning espresso every day would cost 60 million to 70 million rials ($32-$38) a month. Jobs shrank as prices rose. Employment fell approximately 450,000 year-on-year (to 24.67M), unemployment rose to 2.5 million, and 1.3 million full-time jobs vanished, NIAC Insights reported. The industry took a major hit, with approximately 629,000 jobs lost. Gholamhossein Mohammadi, a deputy labour minister, said in April that the war had, by preliminary estimate, directly destroyed more than one million jobs and left roughly two million people unemployed once indirect effects were counted. Iran's declining purchasing power: Impact on dairy, meat and coffee consumption Soaring food prices are reshaping what Iranian families eat. Earlier in August, figures showed a steep decline in dairy consumption alongside a longer retreat from red meat. Experts have warned that ending the war with the US could expose Iran to one of its greatest vulnerabilities. They believe that Tehran stares at a battered post-war economy that may strain its ability to finance the institutions underpinning its rule. "If the conflict ends today, then you're going to see the economic effect of the war doing its work," former US Treasury official and sanctions strategist Miad Maleki told Eye for Iran. "That would be very scary if I was an Iranian regime official, having to face the reality of a post-war economy," Maleki was quoted as saying. Maleki said the greater danger to the regime may emerge once the fighting stops and it must govern a country burdened by soaring inflation, reconstruction costs and years of economic decline. The question, he says, is no longer simply whether the government can continue paying salaries, but whether those salaries still buy enough to sustain loyalty. title: India Q1 GDP growth seen at 7.3% as consumption, capex cushion Iran war shock: ET poll
content:
Gross domestic product likely grew by a median 7.3%, showed an ET poll of 10 economists, with estimates ranging from 6.7% to 8%. RBI pegged June quarter growth at 7%. The economy grew 7.8% in the March quarter and 6.8% in Q1FY26. The National Statistical Office (NSO) will release official GDP data for Q1 on August 31.
“High frequency indicators across the industrial and services sectors have revealed a healthy picture of domestic volume growth in Q1FY27,” said ICRA’s chief economist Aditi Nayar.
“They belie the concerns of a fallout of the West Asia conflict in the quarter,” said Nayar.
Radhika Rao, senior economist and executive director at DBS Bank, said corporate earnings indicators were also broadly constructive, with aggregate revenue growth across listed firms remaining resilient, though higher energy prices crimped profitability at oil marketing companies.
Investment activity strengthened, with the Centre’s capital expenditure rising 18.6% in Q1FY27, compared with 9.1% in the previous quarter.
“Manufacturing activity remained buoyant, supported by strong volume growth,” said Sakshi Gupta, principal economist at HDFC Bank. “The squeeze on profit margins has been offset by the increase in volume sales.”
Nayar however said elevated input costs likely weighed on profitability across some sectors, and consequently value-added growth in the quarter, compressing GDP expansion.
Services activity remained buoyant, with the services purchasing managers’ index rising to 58.6 on average in Q1FY27 from 58 in the previous quarter. Services exports also accelerated to 13.1% from 8.9% over the same period.
Rajani Sinha, chief economist at CareEdge Ratings, said sectors such as agriculture, public administration and trade, hotels, transport, communication and services related to broadcasting services could be a drag on the overall growth momentum in Q1, due to the likely impact of elevated energy prices and subdued travel activity amid the escalated geopolitical tensions.
She said agricultural growth is likely to be impacted by the delayed onset of the monsoon and softer agricultural activity during the quarter.
Economists expect the strong performance in the fiscal first quarter to be followed by some moderation in the second and third quarters of FY27, as the fallout of the Iran war feeds through, and high raw material and energy prices dampen activity.
Economists are likely to revise their FY27 growth projections upwards following the stronger-than-expected momentum in the first quarter. The ET poll puts the median FY27 GDP growth estimate at around 6.8%, with forecasts ranging from 6.5% to 7.5%.
CareEdge Ratings has already revised its FY27 GDP growth forecast to 7% from 6.7%. DBS Bank sees an upside bias to its estimate, while Kotak Mahindra Bank is also likely to revise its forecast to 7%.
However, weather-related and geopolitical uncertainties remain key risks to the outlook.
“The spatial and temporal distribution of rainfall during the remainder of the season will be critical,” said Sinha. “On the external front, continued volatility in global energy prices remains a key risk factor.”
The World Bank and International Monetary Fund (IMF) pegged India’s FY27 growth at 6.6% and 6.4%, respectively. As per their estimates, India remains among the world’s fastest-growing major economies.

title: India opens tax amnesty scheme for small taxpayers to declare select foreign assets
content:
Announced by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman in the February 1 Budget, the one-time scheme is aimed at bringing certain previously undisclosed foreign assets and income into the tax net, particularly benefiting small taxpayers including students and non-resident Indians.
Under the scheme, taxpayers with undisclosed foreign income of up to Rs 1 crore can make a declaration until December 31, 2026. They will be required to pay tax at 30% of the undisclosed income, along with an equal amount as penalty.
The scheme also covers taxpayers who acquired foreign assets worth up to Rs 5 crore using income on which tax had already been paid but failed to report those assets in their income tax returns.

title: Centre to select first 50 airports under modified UDAN scheme
content:
The Centre will soon select the first batch of 50 airports for development under the modified UDAN scheme as it invites nominations from State and Union Territory governments, sources told businessline.
The Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA) will evaluate the proposals under a challenge mode framework before finalising the first set of 50 airports for infrastructure development.
The selection exercise forms part of the modified UDAN scheme, which envisages the development of 100 airports and aerodromes over the next eight years through the upgradation of existing unserved airstrips at an estimated capital outlay of ₹12,159 crore.
The Centre has earmarked ₹3,661 crore for the construction of 200 helipads, primarily in hilly, island, remote and aspirational regions, as it seeks to strengthen regional air connectivity across the country.
Under the revised framework, State and Union Territory governments will nominate unserved airstrips, heliports and water aerodromes within their jurisdictions for consideration under the scheme. The Airports Authority of India (AAI), acting as the implementing agency, along with MoCA, will then assess the nominated locations before selecting airports for development.
The nominated sites will be evaluated on parameters including availability of 100 per cent encumbrance-free land, existing infrastructure readiness, technical and airspace feasibility, projected passenger traffic, regional connectivity requirements and tourism potential.
Apart from physical infrastructure, the evaluation will also consider commitments by State governments to provide operational support, including concessional electricity and water supply, free security and firefighting services and a value-added tax (VAT) on Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) capped at a maximum of 1 per cent.
Furthermore, the scheme provides ₹2,577 crore as operational and maintenance support to facilitate the operationalisation of Regional Connectivity Scheme (RCS)-only airports during the initial years of operation.
The financial assistance will be available for the first three years and will be capped at ₹3.06 crore annually for each airport and ₹0.90 crore annually for each heliport or water aerodrome.
According to sources, the support will cover a certain percentage of expenditures related to staffing for Communication, Navigation and Surveillance/Air Traffic Management (CNS/ATM), meteorological services, among others, at up to 441 airports, heliports and water aerodromes.
Besides infrastructure and operational support, the modified UDAN framework also provides airport charge exemptions for Regional Connectivity Scheme flights. These include waiver of landing, parking and passenger-related airport charges, exemption from Terminal Navigation Landing Charges and discounted Route Navigation Facility Charges, aimed at improving the commercial viability of regional air services.

title: FinMin nudges ministries to switch to producer price index for rate adjustments in govt contracts
content:
The finance ministry has nudged all ministries and departments to move to Producer Price Index (PPI), from the current Wholesale Price Index (WPI), for rate escalation and adjustment clauses in future government procurement contracts.
The Department of Expenditure, in a communication to all ministries and departments, said that PPI is a more internationally accepted index compared to WPI used in government contracts to define price escalation.
For the first time, the commerce ministry has started issuing monthly PPI data for both goods and services since June to better reflect price movement at the producer's level, thus paving the way for phasing out wholesale price inflation numbers in the next five years.
"Ministries/Departments are encouraged to adopt Producer Price Index (PPI) in place of Wholesale Price Index (WPI) in all price escalation clauses of future contracts, once PPI becomes available," the expenditure department said in an office memorandum dated July 13, which was sent to all ministries.
The price escalation or rate variation clause in government contracts allows payments to be adjusted in line with changes in the cost of key inputs, such as materials, labour and fuel, during the execution of a project. It helps distribute the impact of inflation between the government and the contractor.
The launch of monthly PPI data is in line with practices adopted by advanced economies and follows the recommendations of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which stressed that India needs to transition from WPI to PPI.
The output (goods) PPI cover all representative goods transacted in the economy. Manufactured items have the highest 69.93 per cent weight in output PPI (goods), followed by agriculture, forestry and fishing (22.16 per cent), electricity (4.49 per cent), and mining and quarrying (3.42 per cent).

title: From farm to bottle: How agriculture powers India’s beverage economy
content:
India’s farms just delivered a record. The Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare’s Second Advance Estimates, released in June this year, put the country’s total horticulture production at 377.78 million tonnes for 2025-26, with fruit output alone rising 3.25 per cent to 121.48 million tonnes, led by banana, mango, papaya, apple and guava.
Numbers like these tend to get filed under agriculture news and forgotten by the time anyone reaches for a juice carton. They shouldn’t be.
Every one of those tonnes is a potential input for an industry that spends most of its time talking about flavours, packaging and shelf space, and very little time talking about where its raw material actually comes from.
That is a mistake worth correcting, because the beverage business is, underneath the branding, a farm business wearing better clothes. A juice or RTD tea brand does not create fruit, sugar or water. It aggregates them, processes them and sells the result at a margin that depends entirely on how reliably those inputs show up. A record harvest is not a footnote for this industry. It is the year’s most important supply chain event, arguably more consequential than any single product launch.
What a good harvest actually buys you
The temptation in a year like this is to treat abundance as permanent. It is not. Fruit output has grown for several years running, helped by government investment in irrigation, cold chain and processing infrastructure under schemes like Operation Greens, which now covers 22 perishables instead of the tomato, onion and potato it started with. But orchards do not scale the way factories do. A mango tree takes years to mature, a cold chain gap in one district can undo a season’s gains, and a single bad monsoon can reverse three years of steady growth overnight. The companies that treat a good year as licence to relax on sourcing relationships are the ones caught flat-footed when the next difficult one arrives. The companies that use a good year to lock in longer contracts, deepen farmer partnerships and invest in aggregation infrastructure are the ones still standing when it does not.
This is not an abstract concern. India’s non-alcoholic beverages market was valued at $14.95 billion in 2024 and is projected to grow at 7.36 per cent a year through 2030, according to the Ministry of Food Processing Industries. That growth will not be won on marketing spend alone. It will be won by whoever has methodically built the most dependable supply chain between farm and bottling line, because consumers are increasingly discerning about where a “real fruit” or “natural” claim actually comes from, and that scrutiny only grows as the market does.
Water deserves the same long view
The same discipline applies to water, arguably more urgently. The Central Ground Water Board’s own data shows real progress here, with the share of India’s groundwater assessment units rated “safe” rising from 62.6 per cent in 2017 to 73.4 per cent in 2024. That is a genuine national achievement, built on years of recharge programmes and better monitoring. But a beverage company drawing from a single aquifer cannot afford to read a national average as a local guarantee. The responsible read of that improvement is not relief, it is a reminder that water stewardship has to be as deliberate and long-term as sourcing strategy, tracked block by block rather than assumed from the top line.
None of this makes for an easy headline. But the industries that will still be growing a decade from now are the ones treating agriculture as core infrastructure today, not as a line item to revisit when a harvest disappoints. This year’s numbers are good. What matters more is what gets built while they are.
The author is Joint Managing Director, SLMG Beverages

title: Congress protests in Kalaburagi against ‘purification’ ritual at Kharge’s rally venue in Uttarakhand
content:
The Kalaburagi District Congress Committee staged a protest in the city on Sunday condemning the alleged ‘purification’ ritual performed at a venue in Haldwani, Uttarakhand, where Congress president and Leader of the Opposition in the Rajya Sabha Mallikarjun Kharge, a Dalit leader, had addressed a public meeting.
The protest came days after Mr. Kharge raised the issue in the Rajya Sabha, describing the incident as a reflection of the persistence of untouchability and caste discrimination which was prohibited in the Constitution. The controversy had erupted after a ritual was reportedly conducted at the Ramlila Maidan following his August 8 rally. The matter has since triggered a political row, with the government promising the Rajya Sabha that the allegation would be looked into.
The Congress protest began from the party’s district office off Sedam Road and culminated near Annapurna Cross. Party workers raised slogans against the Bharatiya Janata Party, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh and what they described as communal and casteist tendencies. They also burnt tyres as a mark of protest.
The protesters carried placards carrying slogans such as “80 years of Independence, has casteism still not gone?”, “The Constitution is our religion and equality is its goal”, “Purification should be of the mind, not by caste”, “Before cleansing the soil, cleanse your minds” and “Hail unity, condemn hatred”.
District Congress Committee president and MLC Jagdev Guttedar, MLA Allamaprabhu Patil, and another MLC Tippannappa Kamaknoor addressed the protesters.
MLA of Kalaburagi North Kaneez Fatima, Kalaburagi Urban Development Authority chairman Mazhar Alam Khan, former Minister Revu Naik Belamagi, district president of the Five Guarantee Committee Chandrika Parameshwar, District Mahila Congress president Renuka Singe, District Youth Congress president Shakeel Ahmed Saradagi and party leaders Dr Kiran Deshmukh, Rajiv Jane, Subhash Rathod and Bhimrao T.T. were among those who participated in the protest along with hundreds of party workers.

title: Rejuvenation of irrigation channels, ponds to begin in Tamil Nadu under VB-G RAM G scheme
content:
As part of the preparedness for the northeast monsoon, the Rural Development and Panchayat Raj Department will begin rejuvenation of 10,185 irrigation channels and 809 ponds across Tamil Nadu, starting on Monday (August 17, 2026).
The rejuvenation works will be taken up under the Viksit Bharat – Gramin Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (VB-G RAM G) scheme. According to sources, desilting of water bodies and irrigation channels ahead of the northeast monsoon will help store rainwater to its capacity, raise the groundwater table and improve irrigation facilities for agriculture. Further, it will help flood control during periods of heavy rainfall.
These works are set to commence on Monday (August 17, 2026) in 37 districts, excluding Chennai, at an estimated cost of ₹507.92 crore. Minister for Rural Development and Water Resources N. Anand is scheduled to inaugurate the works. The desilting works will be launched by Ministers and MLAs in their respective rural areas in the coming days, sources added.
Mr. Anand told The Hindu that the desilting of ponds, ooranis, and channels would be taken up after due measurement by surveyors. The department will coordinate with farmers, panchyat representatives, and volunteering agencies that work with channels and water bodies and ensure the work is done properly. The payment will be done only after the work is completed. “At the same time, since in some places persons with disabilities are also part of the VB- G RAM G, we will ensure that they are not disturbed in any manner. The work will be completed by September-end, when the monsoon is likely to begin,” he said.
Since the entire work cannot be done manually, we have sought corporate social responsibility funds for earth movers and other machinery. The Minister, who is also TVK party general secretary, said party workers will also take part in the efforts to desilt and clear bushes from the channels. “Anyone willing to volunteer can join in the efforts.”
Farmers with whom The Hindu spoke, said though this was a welcome idea, VB-G RAM G workers alone would not be able to complete the work on their own. “In some villages, especially in the Delta districts, farmers come together to desilt channels. In such cases, the government’s desilting work can be clubbed with ours to make it more effective,” said Ravichandran, a farmer of Nannilam.
A total of 2,514 channels and 53 ooranies are to be desilted in Thanjavur alone, and 816 channels in Thoothukudi, 625 in Krishnagiri, and 608 in Villupuram channels are also to be desilted. Ramanathapuram has the highest number of ponds to be desilted with 137, followed by Dindigul with 109 and Madurai with 70.
G RAM G in their areas were not physically fit to perform desilting work. “It will only be a waste of time, energy, and efforts. We have seen these people spending time simply sitting under trees and collecting their wages after doing nothing,” he alleged.

title: Olympics is always the biggest stage: Robles
content:
For more than a decade, Alvaro Robles has been a regular presence on the international table tennis circuit. The Spanish left-hander, who has reached a career-high No. 28 in the world, has spent nearly 10 years inside the top 100 and is now a familiar face in the Ultimate Table Tennis, having featured in six of the seven editions.
Robles’ journey, however, began with an unlikely idol: Timo Boll. As a teenager in Spain, he watched videos of the German great and began copying his game before eventually moving to Germany to train alongside some of the world’s best.
That decision, he says, shaped not only his table tennis but also his personality.
Now a father of two, Robles continues to juggle the demands of a professional career with family life while trying to earn another shot at the Olympics.
In an interaction with The Hindu, he spoke about Boll, his move to Germany, the evolution of Spanish table tennis, longevity in the sport, UTT’s impact on Indian table tennis and his desire to feature in another Olympics. Excerpts:
You have spoken about Boll being one of your idols. How did that fascination begin?
I started watching him when I was 16 or 17. He was in his prime and I watched so many of his matches. I took a lot of motivation from his game. I think my style is quite similar to his.
Was there a particular moment that got you hooked to his style?
What I remember most is that when I was 16 or 17, we started getting access to computers and I watched the first videos on YouTube. I was very impressed. I started copying him in practice and tried to take every skill from him as a left-hander. As you said, it was natural for many lefties to copy Boll.
You then moved to Germany. Did you get an opportunity to interact with him?
Not very often, but a few times. I played against him and practised with him. It was a privilege to share those moments with somebody I really admired. I could never beat him — he was so good — but I managed to have some close matches. I was very happy about that.
How much did moving to Germany transform your career?
It had a huge impact on my career and table tennis. I got to know the best players in the world and learnt more about training systems, how other players think and what mentality is required to reach the top.
How difficult was it as a teenager to take that decision?
It was a difficult choice. When you decide to move, you don’t know the consequences or what you will face. But it was a beautiful journey to discover. If I look back, I would do it again. I met people from all around the world... different countries and cultures. I am really happy to have experienced that kind of life.
Was it tough for your family to understand why you wanted to move to Germany?
In Spain, there was not much of a tradition for table tennis. My parents supported me, but I am not sure they knew exactly what kind of future I would have. I am grateful for their support and the freedom they gave me because that allowed me to develop my career, my personality and my character. I discovered so much about myself during that journey.
How much has Spanish table tennis changed over the last two decades?
It has developed a lot. I think we have been very successful in improving the medium level of players. Now we have around 20 players competing at a very similar level. They are not yet at the top level, but many are between 100 and 300 in the world and can compete really well.
The next step is obviously to have more players inside the top 100. But even at the base, we have some amazing under-13, under-15 and under-17 players achieving unbelievable international results.
If a Spanish teenager came to you today saying he wanted to make a career in table tennis, what would you tell him?
First, it is very important to understand the background of each player — where they come from, which club they belong to, how old they are and what they want to achieve. Everyone is individual and different. That is the first thing I would observe before giving any advice. I would like to know the background of each player so I can help them better.
You have spent almost a decade in the world’s top 100. How demanding is that consistency?
It is very demanding. For 10 years I have been inside the top 100, and it costs a lot. In my case, the secret is consistency in the work. I thought about my practice, physical condition and performance every day. I was worried about improving every day and maybe that is why I have remained around the top 50. Now I am No. 67, but before the Olympics, I reached No. 28, which was great for my career. I keep thinking every day about how I can return to my best shape. I hope I can remain at this level for another 10 years.
Players are now extending their careers well into their late 30s and 40s. How has that become possible?
A few things have changed. There are now many opportunities to continue playing WTT events and league matches. There are great leagues where players can earn an income. To perform for many years, there is much more information about taking care of yourself — nutrition, physical preparation and psychology. Earlier, many players didn’t have access to so much information.
Because of this, we feel better with our bodies, play with fewer injuries and continue believing that we can play at 38, 40 or 42. Then it comes down to your mental approach, motivation, circumstances, family and how long you want to keep travelling. Look at Robert Gardos, who is 47 and still performing extremely well. That is impressive, but it is also because he takes great care of himself.
How would you compare the support structure in Spain with countries such as Germany or Sweden, or India?
Support is not only about money. For me, support means having a structure of coaches and people who help develop the sport — physical trainers, analysts, physiotherapists and people guiding players towards their maximum potential.
Sometimes we are confused. Support is not simply ‘I give you money and then you do what you want.’ Support is creating a structure that helps a group reach its potential. That is what is improving now.
How difficult is it to balance travelling for seven months a year with family life?
It is difficult. I have travelled abroad for six or seven months a year, and it is hard when you know your family is at home. My children are young and they miss me.
We try to manage the logistics so they can come to some tournaments. My daughter came to the World Championships in Doha last year and they came to a Contender in Macedonia. That gives me energy because being away from home for so many weeks is difficult. Bringing them with me and having them around gives me motivation to keep trying for my best results.
How has fatherhood changed the approach to your career?
Totally. Even though I thought I would manage it one way, everything changed because the feelings are different. Suddenly, you have to face things you are not prepared for and manage them with your wife and family.
more than table tennis: learning how to handle family life with professional life.
You have been part of UTT for six seasons. How have you seen the league evolve?
Quite well. The idea was to create a league where foreign players could bring experience to Indian table tennis. Now you see how much Indian table tennis has grown. It is crazy.
If you compare 2018 with 2026, you can now see how many Indian players are in the top 100, top 50 and top 40. Youngsters play as if they have 20 years of experience.
Earlier, you didn’t see that. Now there are many of them. That has come from the investment and effort of the federation and the people who wanted to create the league. It is very impressive.
You see youngsters such as Syndrela Das, who was watching from the stands when she was 11 or 12, now playing against players like Manika Batra and even beating them. That comes from a country’s big effort to develop a sport.
What do you enjoy doing away from table tennis?
I love sport. I like playing tennis, padel and football. All my hobbies are related to sport. Going out with my wife when the kids are not with us is also something I enjoy — going on holiday after many months of hard work. That is how I switch off and recharge.
You have won a World championship doubles silver and a European mixed doubles gold. What remains the biggest target?
The European championship gold in mixed doubles is a great achievement because, at the end, it is a gold medal. It is very special to me. But the Olympics is always the biggest stage. Everything I am doing is aimed at getting that experience one more time. I know winning an Olympic medal is something really, really difficult... on another level.
But I try to find my best version and keep the opportunity open. You never know. I will keep fighting to be there and give my best version one more time.

title: Ever-hungry Sindhu targets record sixth Worlds medal
content:
time World championships medallist P.V. Sindhu will look for a record-breaking sixth prize as she begins her campaign here on Monday. A half dozen medals will make her the first women’s singles player to achieve the feat in the tournament.
Fresh from ending a long wait for a title at the Japan Open, Sindhu said the triumph had given her the confidence for the World championships. “It has been quite good, physically and mentally. I have been able to see the changes in terms of my game and my movement,” she said.
One thing that has remained throughout her career, she said, is her “hunger towards the game”.
“I know it is in me and I can still do it.”
But the game has evolved, with women’s singles becoming more demanding. “Women’s singles used to be more attacking and fast-paced. Now it is more about long rallies, patience and staying on court for a longer period,” she said.
Experience, she added, has helped her deal with conditions that can force players to alter their style.
“I’m much more experienced now in terms of how to deal with different conditions on court.
“Sometimes there is drift, and sometimes you cannot control the shuttle the way you want.
“You have to change accordingly and make things convenient for yourself.”
The home setting brings added expectations, but the pressure that comes with playing a high-stakes match is nothing new to her.
“I have played a lot of first-round matches where I had butterflies and there is a lot of pressure… at the same time, there is nothing to lose. I just want to give my best because I have trained hard and I have worked hard in my training session”.

title: HOCKEY WORLD CUP | India’s inexperience hurts it in a stalemate against China
content:
It was a game of two halves with India dominating the opening 30 minutes, before China turned the tables to assert why it is ranked five places above its Asian rival.
India had eight World Cup debutants on show, who played with youthful zest but the inexperience ultimately hurt it in its 2-2 draw against China in its Women’s World Cup Pool D opener here at the Wagener Stadion on Sunday.
India deservedly went 2-1 ahead at the break after goals from Navneet Kaur and Deepika. India’s vertical approach, through the wings, troubled China’s backline as Deepika and Lalremsiami, in particular, looked dangerous with their dribbling and close control.
The opening goal came in the seventh minute when Neha fired in a pass to Navneet, which she deftly guided past several feet into the bottom corner of the goal.
But a poor foul inside the circle by defender Shilpi Dabas, playing only her sixth senior game, in the dying seconds of the first quarter, allowed China to get on the scoresheet from a Ying Zhang penalty stroke.
At the end of the first quarter tactical team talk, India responded to Sjoerd Marijne’s animated instructions by outplaying China.
Every time China looked to play out of its own half, the Indian players swarmed around them, snapping at them, to win the ball and force a turnover. In the 24th minute, Deepika’s mazy run into the circle, earned India its third Penalty Corner, from which she converted.
But early in the second half, the warning signs started to ring for the Indian team. China cut out India’s outlet of playing the ball out from the flanks and pinned it in its own half.
China’s gangly midfielder Li Hong asserted herself, dictating play, before it restored parity for the second time from a rasping dragflick from Ma Ning.
In the last two quarters, China had 13 circle penetrations to India’s three, while adding four PC opportunities to restrict India to none. Savita Punia made crucial interventions as India hung for a valuable point.
The Indian men’s team will take on England in its second Pool D game on Monday.

title: IND vs SL Test Day 2: Padikkal and Jurel consolidate India’s position on rain-hit day
content:
Sunday was largely about waiting for the sun. Fringed by the Indian Ocean and lashed by monsoon winds, Galle woke up to the pitter-patter of rains and birdsong. Umbrellas were out, puddles were the norm and the moist climate had a distinct bearing on the first Test as play resumed well after the lunch break.
Undeterred by the damp skies, India pursued its ambition of posting a healthy first-innings total against Sri Lanka. The goal was achieved with Devdutt Padikkal and Dhruv Jurel lending a hand at varying points. And at close of the second day here at the Galle International Stadium, Shubman Gill’s men scored 460 for nine in 116 overs.
Conscious about inclement weather making further intrusions into the remainder of the Test, and resuming at the overnight 288 for two, India sought urgent runs. Centurion Padikkal continued unhindered while Rishabh Pant lashed left-arm spinner Prabath Jayasuriya for four.
The host skipper Dhananjaya de Silva quickly sought the new ball and employed pace and spin in tandem. Pant miscued a hoick off Keshara Nuwantha, and K.L. Rahul returned to the crease. Rahul, however, had a brief tenure and succumbed to Nuwantha for 82 (175b, 10x4, 1x6) as the debutant off-spinner found turn and appreciable bounce. At the other end Padikkal went past 150 with a whipped four off seamer Asitha Fernando.
With Jurel for company, Padikkal (167, 230b, 15x4, 1x6) was busy shifting gears when he got stumped off Prabath. Ravindra Jadeja strode in and he too preferred flamboyance over dogged resistance. Even as he departed, Jurel extended India’s quest for a 400-plus score. He hoisted Nuwantha for six.
There is a calm air that Jurel always exudes, and he became the lower-order spine. Along with Manav Suthar, he hustled the runs. It needed a sharp catch from Dhananjaya stationed at first slip for Jurel (51, 68b, 4x4, 1x6) to depart after he prodded at Prabath. Mohammed Siraj jauntily walked in, hit a six, played and missed, and even as the tail wobbled, India would like to believe that it has enough to dominate this opening fixture.
Earlier, persistent rains washed away the first session. The persevering ground-staff did their best but with dark clouds often rolling in, they had a daunting task of keeping the turf dry. Like the ‘Myth of Sisyphus’, their effort seemed akin to rolling a boulder uphill.
Coach Gautam Gambhir and batting coach Sitanshu Kotak stepped out and inspected the outfield. Bowling coach Morne Morkel bonded with fellow South African and current Sri Lankan coach Gary Kirsten. And finally when play was about to resume, another wet spell forced the players to hurry back to the pavilion.
Thankfully, the sun enforced its will and the game commenced at 2.35 p.m., and it was India’s turn to press forward in a contest that is bound to be held hostage by brooding skies. There is a forecast for more rains in the coming days and every session will be crucial.

title: British Indian Amit Bhatia-led consortium agrees to acquire minority stake in Liverpool F.C.
content:
Premier League side Liverpool F.C. has entered into a "definitive agreement" to sell a minority equity stake to a consortium led and managed by British-Indian businessman Amit Bhatia, with Amazon founder Jeff Bezos among the prominent investors.
46-year-old Amit Bhatia, son-in-law of Indian steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, leads and manages 1892 Holdings, which also includes K5 Sports, a K5 Global Fund with Bezos as its lead investor, and EE Capital, the family office of Elaine and Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin.
"Fenway Sports Group (FSG), a global sports, media, entertainment and real estate company, today announced that it has entered into a definitive agreement for the sale of a minority equity stake in Liverpool FC to 1892 Holdings," a club statement read.
Existing owners Fenway Sports Group, however, will retain majority ownership and operational control of Liverpool, with the strategic investment aimed at supporting the club's long-term growth ambitions.
"We are incredibly proud to be investing in Liverpool Football Club and to be doing so alongside FSG. We have the utmost respect and admiration for FSG as owners and for everything they have achieved at Anfield," Mr. Bhatia said in a statement.
"To be welcomed as a partner in a club of this stature is a huge privilege. We are making this investment because we believe deeply in Liverpool and its leadership, and we look forward to supporting the club’s continued success for years to come," he added.
FSG president Mike Gordon said the consortium shared the group's long-term philosophy and appreciation of Liverpool's identity.
"As we considered this opportunity, it became clear that Amit and the consortium shared our long-term philosophy and appreciation for what makes Liverpool special," FSG president Mike Gordon said.
"Their experience and perspective will complement the strong foundation already in place, and we look forward to working together." The investment also brings together prominent figures from the global business and technology sectors, including Bezos, Saverin along with the Mittal family.
based FSG had acquired Liverpool in 2010 for 300 million pounds and has overseen a period of significant success, including the club's Premier League title in 2020 and its sixth Champions League triumph in 2019.

title: Barcelona finally get Rodri after third offer as Man City accept €76.5m deal
content:
Barcelona have reportedly reached an agreement in principle to sign Rodri from Manchester City, with the Spain captain set to return to La Liga after seven trophy-filled seasons in England.
The proposed deal is understood to be worth €76.5 million (about $88.4 million) in total, after Barcelona returned with a third offer for the 30-year-old midfielder. Rodri is set to sign a four-year contract with the La Liga champions. The move would bring one of the world's most accomplished midfielders back to Spain just weeks after he captained the country to the 2026 World Cup and was named the tournament's best player.
Barcelona return with third offer
Barcelona had already seen two approaches for Rodri rejected before returning with an improved proposal over the weekend.
According to sources cited by ESPN and
, Barcelona’s third offer takes the total package to €76.5 million ($88.4m). City will receive an upfront €60 million ($68.8m), with more than €11 million in highly achievable bonuses, and the Premier League club expects to receive at least €71.5 million overall for Rodri, who has less than 12 months left on his contract.
Rodri is expected to travel to Barcelona in the coming days and could be presented before Wednesday's Joan Gamper Trophy match against Al Ahly at Spotify Camp Nou.
The agreement follows a summer in which Rodri's future had become increasingly uncertain. He was entering the final year of his Manchester City contract, giving the English club a reason to consider a sale if the right offer arrived.
Barcelona's interest also developed after Frenkie de Jong suffered a long-term injury, prompting the Spanish champions to explore the midfield market more seriously.
Rodri was not initially considered a priority target, but his availability changed the picture. Barcelona then moved ahead with their pursuit, while sources told ESPN that the midfielder preferred a return to Spain with Barça over a move to Real Madrid.
A statement signing for Barcelona
Barcelona see Rodri as a major addition to a squad that has won consecutive Spanish league titles and are understood to view him as a player capable of strengthening Hansi Flick's side for the coming seasons.
His arrival would also add another established leader to a summer recruitment drive that has already brought Anthony Gordon, Karim Adeyemi and Jesse Bisiwu to the club.
João Cancelo is also set to return to Barcelona as a free agent, according to sources cited by ESPN, while the club continue to pursue a striker. Atlético Madrid's Julián Álvarez is their leading target following the departures of
and Ferran Torres.
Rodri's experience would be particularly valuable in a squad preparing to compete on multiple fronts. He has won at the highest level in both club and international football, while his ability to control games from midfield has made him one of the defining players in his position.
Rodri leaves City after seven seasons
Rodri joined Manchester City from Atlético Madrid in 2019 after previously playing for Villarreal and Atlético.
Across 298 appearances in seven seasons, he helped City win 12 major honours, including four Premier League titles, two FA Cups, three EFL Cups and the Champions League in 2022-23.
His time in England was interrupted by a serious knee injury that ruled him out for much of the 2024-25 campaign, while a hamstring problem also disrupted parts of last season.
He returned to his best level at the 2026 World Cup, captaining Spain to the title after a 1-0 extra-time victory over Argentina. Rodri was also awarded the Golden Ball as the tournament's best player.
The World Cup triumph followed his success at Euro 2024, where he was also named player of the tournament. That performance helped him win the 2024 Ballon d'Or.
Rodri with the 2024 Ballon d'Or trophy
Rodri would therefore leave Manchester City having added almost every major honour available to his collection.
City prepare for life without their midfield anchor
Barcelona's opening proposal was reportedly rejected last week, with City turning down an offer worth around €45.2 million ($52.2 million) before the Catalan club increased its bid.
After Sunday's Community Shield defeat by Arsenal, new City manager Enzo Maresca acknowledged the difficulty of replacing a player of Rodri's calibre.
“Rodri is a player who just won the World Cup and Ballon d'Or,” Maresca said. “He's a top player, all the teams need a Rodri, so it's not about if we miss Rodri or not.”
Manchester City's Rodri . (AP Photo)
Rodri's departure would bring an end to his seven-year spell at the Etihad and leave City without a midfielder who has been central to their most successful period.
For Barcelona, meanwhile, the agreement would bring home a player who has already won a World Cup, European Championship and Ballon d'Or, while still being 30 years old and entering what could be several important seasons at the Camp Nou.

title: Hockey World Cup: India hold Olympic silver medallists China to 2-2 draw
content:
India began their Women’s FIH Hockey World Cup campaign with a hard-fought 2-2 draw against Paris Olympics silver medallists China on Sunday, twice taking the lead before being forced to settle for a point at the Wagener Hockey Stadium in Amstelveen, Netherlands.
Navneet Kaur gave India an early lead before Zhang Ying equalised from a penalty stroke in the dying seconds of the opening quarter. Deepika then restored India's advantage through a penalty corner in the second quarter, but Ma Ning levelled the contest in the third as China took control of proceedings.
China dominated large periods of the second half and came close to completing the comeback, particularly in the closing stages. India, however, managed to withstand the pressure and secure a valuable point against the highest-ranked side in Pool D.
India vs China, Hockey World Cup
India make bright start, take lead
India began with confidence and looked the sharper side in the opening exchanges, enjoying more possession and making repeated incursions into the Chinese circle.
Their early pressure was rewarded in the eighth minute when Navneet scored from the top of the circle. India had been building promising moves and were rewarded for their positive approach as Navneet reacted quickest to put them ahead.
China gradually increased the tempo after conceding and began creating problems for the Indian defence.
The pressure eventually told in the dying seconds of the first quarter. Shilpi was penalised for a push inside the circle, prompting India to review the decision as they believed she had been pushed by Zhong Jiaqi. The TV umpire upheld the on-field call, leaving India without their review.
Zhang Ying converted the resulting penalty stroke in the 15th minute to make it 1-1.
China started the second quarter with greater authority after the equaliser, but India gradually regained their composure and began putting pressure on the Chinese defence.
India earned two penalty corners in quick succession, with Navneet involved in creating the opportunities. The first was defended, but India remained on the front foot and eventually got their reward in the 25th minute.
flick. The ball struck the shoulder of a Chinese defender and looped over the goalkeeper before finding the net.
The umpires took time to assess the goal before confirming it, but India were eventually back in front at 2-1.
China continued to threaten, but India managed to protect their advantage until half-time.
China dominate after the break
The third quarter, however, belonged almost entirely to China. The Olympic silver medallists came out aggressively and immediately put India under pressure.
Baljeet produced a crucial defensive clearance early in the quarter, while goalkeeper Savita made a superb block soon after to deny China an equaliser.
India were increasingly pinned inside their own half, and their inability to launch attacks of their own became a major concern. China finally found their reward in the 39th minute when Ma Ning converted their first penalty corner to make it 2-2.
China continued to dominate for the remainder of the quarter, while India appeared to retreat into a defensive shell.
The pattern continued into the fourth quarter, with China repeatedly swarming into India's circle. India spent long periods defending and struggled to generate attacking momentum.
With the game entering its final stages, China earned another penalty corner and had a golden opportunity to complete the comeback. The resulting strike, however, went just wide of the goal, allowing India to breathe a huge sigh of relief.
India finally produced a strong attacking spell late in the game, shifting play into the Chinese half and putting their defence under pressure. Lalremsiami also came close to restoring India's lead when she failed to connect with a ball that rolled across the face of the Chinese goal.
China had one final opportunity from another penalty corner, but India held firm to secure the draw.
India will now look to build on the result in their remaining Pool D matches.

title: PV Sindhu turns to sports science, S&C in bid for record sixth Worlds medal
content:
occupied the fourth court in the main hall of the Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium on Saturday. At the other end, she had Ayush Shetty braced with his powerful smashes and blistering forehands. Sindhu broke into a smile the moment Ayush landed one of his big smashes into the net.
A day later, she had Unnati Hooda, another debutant like Ayush, for company on the practice court. The court of choice remained the same as the day before, with instructions from coach Irwansyah Adi Pratama ringing in from the sidelines. Having tried plenty of deceptions and drop shots, she would step away briefly for a water break while keeping the conversations going.
It was early morning, the clock reading 8 am, and the Indian contingent was out and about in full flow ahead of the
, which get underway on Monday. Satwiksairaj Rankireddy-Chirag Shetty, Ayush Shetty, Lakshya Sen and Hariharan Amsakarunan-MR Arjun were all on court, with the clock ticking down on the prestigious tournament.
The limelight, however, remains firmly on ninth seed Sindhu. A five-time World Championships medallist, with one gold, two silvers and two bronzes, the 31-year-old still remains firmly in the mix for the title.
If she does stand atop the podium next Sunday, she will eclipse Zhang Ning as the most decorated shuttler in the women's singles category.
PV Sindhu spars with Ayush Shetty at the Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium. (Photo: Tanuj Lakhina)
Form is also on her side. She won the Japan Open Super 750 in July while reaching the semi-finals in Australia and Malaysia and the quarter-finals in Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia. From World No. 13 at the start of the year, she has climbed four rungs to step inside the top 10.
The biggest factor in this uptick in results has been a sharper focus on sports science and building the right team around herself. Wayne Lombard, who has worked with Indian athletes in hockey and boxing and with runner Jyothi Yarraji, helms the strength and conditioning group alongside physio Heera Mundluru and Shreyasi Sanjay.
"It was very important for me to have a Sports Science team around me... in terms of the S&C and the physio. And of course the coach is always there. Wayne (Lombard) heads the strength and conditioning. And of course Heera (Mundluru) is my physio right now. And Shreyasi (Sanjay) looks after the S&C. So I think it's very important that you build around that. Because sometimes your body is not at 100%. But you still push. And injuries just don't tell you and come. It just happens," she told the media on Sunday.
I think physically and mentally, it's been quite good. I'm able to actually see the changes in terms of my game and my movement.
"Before that, what are the precautions that you take and how smartly you change? Because you have all these gadgets now to record your strain, how tired you are, or whether you can push yourself or not. So I think these are some metrics where you make sure and take precautions. So these are the small things that you change.
"And I think that's what helped me. I think physically and mentally, it's been quite good. I'm able to actually see the changes in terms of my game and my movement. So I think I'm happy that it's going in the right way," she continued.
PV Sindhu banking on experience to win sixth medal
It has, however, been seven years since Sindhu won a medal at the BWF World Championships. In that one-sided final, the Hyderabadi beat Nozomi Okuhara for her first gold medal after winning two bronze medals (2013, 2014) and two silvers (2017, 2018).
"In terms of the game and in terms of how you think and how you strategise," she said when asked how PV Sindhu has evolved in the last seven years. "And altogether, the game, badminton as a sport itself, has changed, is what I feel. Earlier, women's singles was more attacking and more of a faster-paced game. But now it's more of long rallies and staying on court for a longer period of time. And, you know, the longer duration that you stay on court, so I think you need a lot of patience in terms of that.
"But when you look back since then until now, yes, as a person, I think in terms of experience, there have been a lot of changes. And I feel now I'm much more experienced, irrespective of playing sport for a longer period of time. I think I'm definitely much more experienced in terms of how to deal on court.
"Sometimes there is drift, sometimes how do you control the shuttle or, you know, it might not go according to you all the time. So, how do you change and make sure that is convenient for you? I think these are a few things that have changed in this period," she continued.
I've played a lot of first-round matches where I had butterflies and there's a lot of pressure. And I won't deny that there is no pressure. There is pressure.
Even though a lot has changed since the first medal in Guangzhou in 2013, she admits that the hunger is the one constant. Despite 15 years of experience and two Olympic medals, she still gets butterflies in her stomach.
"I've played a lot of first-round matches where I had butterflies and there's a lot of pressure. And I won't deny that there is no pressure. There is pressure. But at the same time, for me, there's nothing to lose. And I just want to give my best because I know I have trained hard and I've worked hard in my training sessions," she explained.
"So I just have to go out there onto the court and just, like, just give that and just put my best out there, irrespective of whatever the result is," she continued.
New Delhi, Aug 16 (ANI): Badminton player PV Sindhu speaks during a press conference at the BWF World Championship 2026 at Indira Gandhi Arena Stadium, in New Delhi on Sunday. (ANI Photo/Naveen Sharma)
Even though the 31-year-old went past Chen Yu Fei and Akane Yamaguchi on the way to the title in Japan, the draw isn't the easiest at the BWF World Championships. After starting against Ireland's Sophia Noble, the job gets tougher with Wang Zhi Yi on a collision course in the Round of 16. Zhi Yi has beaten Sindhu thrice this year. If she crosses that hurdle, there is a potential quarter-final against Putri Kusuma Wardani. The Indonesian beat Sindhu at last year's World Championships.
young stands on the opposite side of the draw, and they can meet in the semi-finals. The on-the-mend Korean holds a massive 10-0 head-to-head advantage over Sindhu.
The scoring system is going to be different. It is going to be very challenging. If it was 21 points, there is still time. Like, you are 0-7 down, you still have time to cover. Whereas in 15, if the seven points are done, almost the match is done.
As 24-year-old An Se-young stands well and truly above the rest, despite the injury, the field includes an even mix of veterans and youngsters. Among the 16 seeds, five are under 26 years old, while the rest are older. The 31-year-old Sindhu has seen many come and go, and she would soon see the game evolve into a 15-point format next year.
"I think there is a younger generation who is coming up now in badminton and women's singles especially. The scoring system is going to be different. It is going to be very challenging. If it was 21 points, there is still time. Like, you are 0-7 down, you still have time to cover.
"Whereas in 15, if the seven points are done, almost the match is done. So it is going to be very challenging. And you need to be on your feet from point number one.

title: ‘Unwanted record’: Ex-captain stunned after bizarre blunder by Pak at World Cup
content:
Pakistan's 1-4 defeat to England in their opening Pool D match at the FIH Men's Hockey World Cup 2026 was compounded by an embarrassing moment involving captain Abu Bakar Mahmood, who was shown a green card after his team failed to produce the required protective gear for a penalty corner.
The bizarre incident in the 17th minute, shortly after England had taken a 1-0 lead, left former Pakistan captain Salman Akbar stunned. According to Akbar, Pakistan had forgotten the penalty-corner protective equipment in the changing room, forcing a player to sprint back to retrieve it.
The delay resulted in Abu Bakar being shown a green card and spending two minutes on the sidelines. For Akbar, the incident reflected a deeper problem with preparation and organisation at the highest level of the sport.
“Wow. Another unwanted record from Pakistan hockey. In the opening match of the FIH Hockey World Cup 2026 against England, Pakistan reportedly forgot the penalty corner protective gear in the changing room. As a result, the captain received the green card,” Akbar wrote on X.
‘Simply cannot happen on biggest stage’
Akbar was particularly critical of the fact that such an error occurred during a World Cup match, arguing that preparation extends well beyond tactics and physical fitness.
“Forgetting essential protective equipment for penalty corners simply cannot happen on the biggest stage of international hockey. Preparation is not just about tactics, fitness and skills. It is also about discipline and organisation,” the former captain wrote.
“The World Cup demands the highest level of professionalism. Unfortunately, moments like this raise serious questions about how prepared we really are for the big stage.”
The incident came during a difficult outing for Pakistan, who eventually lost 1-4 to England. The defeat leaves them needing a strong response in their remaining Pool D matches, with India also part of the group.
